title: count = count++
summary: Why assigning a variable to its own postfix increment leaves it unchanged, and what to write instead.
objectives: Explain what value `count++` produces and what it does to `count`.
Trace how `count = count++` changes, or fails to change, a variable.
Replace this mistake with a clear increment.
Recognize the same mistake when another variable name is used.

blocks.text: Suppose `count` is `5`, and you want to increase it by one. It may seem natural to write `count = count++;`. But after this statement, `count` is still `5`, not `6`.

bad.title: The value stays the same

good.title: The value increases

blocks.note: Both programs compile and run. The mistake is not a compile-time error. It is a run-time logic mistake: the first program prints `5` because its assignment puts the old value back into `count`.

blocks.text: The `++` after a variable is called postfix increment. It increases the variable, but the expression itself produces the value from before the increase. In `count = count++;`, the assignment then stores that old value back in `count`.

blocks.caption: What happens when count starts at 5
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Start with count at 5"] --> B["Postfix expression produces old value 5"]
  B --> C["Postfix increment changes count to 6"]
  C --> D["Assignment stores old value 5 in count"]
  D --> E["Final count is 5"]

blocks.title: A useful question
blocks.text: Ask what value the whole expression produces. With `count++`, that value is the old value. Use `count++` by itself when you only want to increase `count`.

sections.title: Trace it, one step at a time

blocks.text: Write down the current value, the value produced by `count++`, and what the assignment stores. This makes it easier to see why the increment does not remain.

blocks.caption: Tracing count = count++ when count starts at 5
rows: The assignment stores the produced value `5` in `count`

blocks.text: The last step is the one to watch. The assignment uses the value produced by the right-hand side, which is the old value `5`. That overwrites the temporary increase.
Here are two ways to apply the trace. In the first, only the final count matters. In the second, the old value is useful too.

bad.title: Trying to increase count

good.title: Increase count directly

blocks.note: In the first program, `count++` produces `2`, and the assignment stores `2` back into `count`. If you only want to increase the variable, write `count++;`.

bad.title: The assignment loses the increase

good.title: Save the old value and keep the increase

blocks.note: Here the old value is useful, so assigning the result of `count++` to a different variable makes sense. In the good version, `oldCount` receives `4` and `count` keeps its new value, `5`.

blocks.text: The variable does not have to be called `count`. Any time you assign a variable to its own postfix increment, the old value is put back. This is valid Java, so the compiler accepts it; the problem shows up when the program runs.

blocks.note: If `score` starts at `10`, the bad statement leaves it at `10`. The good statement leaves it at `11`.
If `count` starts below `3`, the bad loop keeps its value unchanged, so its condition stays true. The good version increases `count` on each pass.

blocks.title: When the old value is needed
blocks.text: Use `int oldCount = count++;` to save the old value in `oldCount` while increasing `count`. Do not assign that result back to `count`.

blocks.question: If `count` starts at `7`, what is its value after `count = count++;`?
blocks.explanation: `count++` produces the old value `7`. The assignment stores `7` back into `count`, so it remains `7`. This is valid Java and compiles.

blocks.question: If `count` starts at `4`, what are the values after `int oldCount = count++;`?
blocks.explanation: Postfix increment produces the old value `4` for the assignment to `oldCount`, then increases `count` to `5`.

blocks.question: You want to increase `total` by one and do not need its old value. Which statement should you use?
blocks.explanation: `total++;` increases `total` directly. The first option assigns the old value back, and `==` asks a question rather than assigning.

items: `count++` is postfix increment: it increases `count` and produces the old value.
`count = count++;` stores the old value back into `count`, so `count` ends unchanged.
This is valid Java. The compiler accepts it, but the result can be wrong when the program runs.
To increase a variable by one, use `count++;` or `count += 1;`.
To save the old value while increasing the variable, use `int oldCount = count++;`.
